blocks.text: Chapter 3.
Circle of Competence
Third night, friend — and it opens with a warning from the poker table.

Warren Buffett loves to quote it: if you've been in the game a while and you still can't spot the patsy... you're the patsy. Every table has one — the player the professionals are quietly feeding on. And here's the cold mechanism behind it: the patsy isn't the dumbest player. He's the one operating outside his circle of competence among people operating inside theirs — and he doesn't know it. Salespeople know this. Negotiators know this. Markets feast on it daily.
Tonight's tool is the one Buffett says built his fortune — and it isn't brilliance, friend. It's a fence.
The perimeter, not the area

Pause and guess: In his 1996 shareholder letter, Buffett described the circle of competence — the domains where your knowledge is deep, earned, reliable. But he added a twist: one property of the circle matters vastly more than another. Which matters — the SIZE of your circle, or something else?
Ready? Here is what happened.

"The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital." A narrow circle honestly mapped beats a vast circle vaguely imagined, friend. Because inside your circle you possess three layers: the nuance practitioners share... knowledge of what you don't know... and even a map of what's unknowable. Outside it, you lack the vocabulary to recognize your own ignorance — you can't ask the right questions, so you can't evaluate the answers you're sold. And catastrophes almost never come from people acting inside their competence and getting unlucky. They come from people who never noticed they crossed the perimeter. Success is the sneakiest trap of all: the brilliant surgeon or founder assumes their judgment transfers to investing or politics — but what actually transferred was only the confidence. The circle is domain-specific, and ego works around the clock to blur the fence line, because "I don't know" feels like a demotion. Flip the incentive, friend: treat the perimeter as the asset. Precision about your ignorance is the skill.

Now meet the two people who make it vivid: the lifer and the stranger. The lifer has spent decades in her small town. She knows which neighbor's promises are worthless, which shortcut floods in spring, the history behind every feud — and, just as important, which local mysteries nobody has ever solved, so she never pays for false certainty. The stranger arrives, looks around for a few days, and concludes the town is simple. Surface mistaken for territory. If they compete on anything that depends on the town — property, business, politics — the lifer wins every time. Not because she's smarter, friend: because she's inside a circle the stranger only thinks he's inside. A weekend of reading makes you a stranger with a guidebook, never a lifer. And the dangerous position isn't being a stranger — everyone is, to most domains. It's being the stranger who believes he's the lifer.
Keeping the fence honest
A circle isn't a diploma, friend — it decays without upkeep while the world changes and memory flatters itself. Three practices keep the map current.

Curiosity — keep learning from experience and, cheaper still, from other people's recorded mistakes; a frozen circle in a moving world is a shrinking one. The decision journal — because memory is a terrible instrument: hindsight quietly rewrites your old forecasts to match whatever happened. So record decisions at the moment you make them — the choice, the reasoning, the variables, what you expect, even how you feel. Review the entries later and the gap between expected and actual outcomes exposes where your thinking is genuinely reliable... and where you've been lucky and calling it skill. Over time, friend, the journal draws your circle's true perimeter in your own handwriting. And third, external feedback — because self-assessment fails exactly where it matters: ego filters the data. Find someone who knows you, will be honest, and whose criticism you'll actually accept — and give them explicit permission to be uncomfortable. That permission is rare, which is precisely why it's an advantage.

But you can't always stay inside the fence — you'll buy houses, face medical choices, navigate careers in territories where you're the stranger. For those days, a three-part protocol: learn the basics — as a phrasebook, not fluency; enough to follow the conversation and detect nonsense, never enough to decide unaided. Consult genuine lifers — vetting them first: real tested expertise, skin in the game, and check their incentives — the person profiting from your decision is not your guide. Then ask for their thought process, not conclusions: how would you think about my situation? what would worry you? And lean on the broad models — the tools of this book travel across domains and catch the categories of error that ignorance lets through. The spirit of the whole protocol, friend: outside your circle, stop trying to be brilliant. Try to avoid being stupid.
The queen who knew what she didn't know

The chapter's grand exhibit wears a crown. 1558: Elizabeth the First takes England's throne — a young queen inheriting a realm religiously fractured, financially strained, ringed by hostile powers. Her reign became one of history's most celebrated. And the secret wasn't omniscience.
Pause and guess: Elizabeth reigned forty-four years and produced a golden age. The chapter's claim: she succeeded because of how she handled the EDGE of her own competence. What did she actually do?
Ready? Here is what happened.

She managed her perimeter like a strategist. Where her judgment was genuinely strong — statecraft, timing, reading people, the theater of authority — she trusted it. For everything else she built a Privy Council of able advisors, most famously William Cecil, and — the rare part — actually listened when counsel contradicted her instincts, instead of gathering flatterers. She was disciplined about restraint too, friend: no expensive foreign adventures, no irreversible commitments in areas where the crown's knowledge and resources ran thin. Stability, solvency, a golden age — produced not by a monarch who knew everything, but by one who knew precisely what she didn't. And the lesson sharpens with rank: power amplifies the ego problem. The more senior you become, the fewer people volunteer the truth, and the easier it is to mistake deference for proof that your circle is enormous. Leaders who last institutionalize the three practices — keep learning, track their own record honestly, and deliberately retain advisors empowered to disagree. The moment of greatest risk never changes: standing just outside the perimeter while believing you're inside it. Knowing which side of the line you're on is the whole game.
Before you go

So: the patsy is whoever's playing outside his circle; Buffett's fence matters for its boundary, not its acreage; the lifer beats the stranger every time — and the stranger-who-thinks-he's-a-lifer beats himself; a journal draws your true perimeter in your own handwriting; and a queen ran a golden age on the strength of knowing what she didn't know.

But a question has been hiding under all three nights so far, friend. Maps, circles — these tell you where your knowledge is good. They don't tell you how to build something new when the maps run out. Tomorrow: the reasoning tool that let a physicist see through a South Pacific island cult of bamboo airplanes... the same tool that asks why five times until convention cracks open and shows what's actually true underneath... and how it turns "impossible" ideas — like growing meat without any animal — into engineering problems. Next time: first principles — thinking from the bedrock up.
Key takeaways
The circle of competence: deep, earned knowledge — and the perimeter matters more than the area (Buffett, 1996).
Outside your circle you can't even ask the right questions — and if you can't spot the patsy at the table, it's you.
The lifer beats the stranger; the fatal position is the stranger who believes he's the lifer.
Maintain the fence: relentless learning, a decision journal that outwits hindsight, and someone licensed to tell you hard truths.
Outside the circle, run the protocol — basics as phrasebook, vetted experts for thought process not conclusions, broad models as guardrails.
Elizabeth I's golden age: power amplifies ego, so institutionalize dissent — knowing which side of the line you're on is the whole game.
